about: People known from history, not from the Bible text: between the Testaments, around the Bible's events, and after the Bible up to 2025 (church councils, Islam, Bible translators, the Reformation, the Bible Students and the Governing Body of Jehovah's Witnesses). tools/build-people.mjs adds them to data/people.js with hist: true. Dates: q 'history' = the year is given in the source publications; 'estimated' = approximate (a clue in the sources, or a year from general histories); 'assumed' = not recorded, placed by generation. 'living': true = no death in the sources; the line runs to the timeline's end. Activity references: '@key' is a source in data/history.js (HISTORY_SOURCES), anything else is a scripture. 'replaces' takes over a person already in the data; 'patch' adds to people already in the data. Write every text in your own words.

people.name: Artaxerxes II
people.summary: Son of Darius II and king of Persia for over 40 years, while Judah was a Persian province. Egypt broke free of Persia in his reign.
events: Becomes king of Persia; Egypt revolts during his reign
His reign ends; his son Artaxerxes III follows him

people.name: Artaxerxes III
people.summary: Remembered as the harshest of the Persian kings. His great achievement was bringing Egypt back under Persian rule.
events: Becomes king of Persia and later wins Egypt back

people.name: Darius III
people.role: Last king of the Persian Empire
people.summary: The last Persian king. Alexander the Great beat his armies at Issus and Gaugamela, and he was killed by his own men soon after, ending the empire that had freed the Jews from Babylon.
people.note: Daniel's vision of a goat overpowering a two-horned ram (Daniel 8:3-7, 20, 21) pictured Greece defeating Medo-Persia.
events: His great army is beaten by Alexander at Issus
Flees and is murdered; the Persian dynasty ends

people.name: Philip II
people.summary: King of Macedonia who brought the Greek city-states under his rule and planned the attack on Persia that his son Alexander carried out.
events: Conquers Greece and unites it under Macedonia
Is murdered; his son Alexander becomes king

people.name: Alexander the Great
people.role: King of Macedonia; conqueror of Persia
people.summary: Became king at 20 and in about ten years swept from Greece through Persia, Egypt and on toward India. With him Greece became the world power, the Greek language spread everywhere, and Judah came under Greek rule. He died at 32, and his empire went to his generals, not his family.
people.note: Not named in the Bible. Daniel foretold a swift conqueror from Greece whose kingdom would be split four ways (Daniel 8:5-8, 21, 22; 11:3, 4).
events: Born at Pella, son of Philip II and Olympias
Crosses into Asia and beats the Persians at the Granicus River
Defeats a vast Persian army at Issus
Uses the rubble of old Tyre to build a causeway and destroys the island city
Takes over Judah. Jewish tradition says the high priest showed him Daniel's prophecy about Greece
Crushes Darius III's army at Gaugamela; the Persian Empire falls

people.name: Antigonus I
people.summary: A one-eyed general of Alexander who tried to take the whole empire for himself after Alexander died. He was killed in battle at Ipsus.
events: Killed at the battle of Ipsus; four of Alexander's generals divide the empire

people.name: Cassander
people.role: General of Alexander; ruler of Macedonia and Greece
people.summary: One of the four generals who divided Alexander's empire. He held Macedonia and Greece and had Alexander's young son killed, so the empire did not pass to Alexander's family.
people.note: Death year from general histories; the sources say only that he died a few years after taking power.
events: Has Alexander's son Alexander IV put to death
Rules Macedonia and Greece, one of four parts of Alexander's empire

people.name: Lysimachus
people.role: General of Alexander; ruler of Asia Minor and Thrace
people.summary: One of the four generals who divided Alexander's empire. He held Asia Minor and Thrace, later took Macedonia too, and fell in battle against Seleucus I.
events: Rules Asia Minor and Thrace, one of four parts of Alexander's empire
Takes the European part of the Greek empire
Falls in battle against Seleucus I

people.name: Ptolemy I
people.role: King of Egypt; the first 'king of the south'
people.summary: A general of Alexander who took Egypt and Palestine and founded the Greek dynasty that ruled Egypt for nearly 300 years. He encouraged Jews to settle in Alexandria and started its famous library. Judah stayed under his family's rule until 198 B.C.E.
people.note: Death year from general histories. His son Ptolemy II began to reign in 285 B.C.E.
events: Draws Jews to settle in Egypt; a large Jewish community grows in Alexandria
Takes the title of king of Egypt
Holds Egypt and Palestine, so Judah is ruled from Egypt

people.name: Ptolemy II
people.role: King of Egypt; 'king of the south'
people.summary: Son of Ptolemy I. In his reign Jewish scholars in Alexandria began translating the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek, the Septuagint. To end a long war with Syria he gave his daughter Berenice to Antiochus II.
events: In his reign, work begins in Alexandria on the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures
Makes peace with Antiochus II by marrying his daughter Berenice to him

people.name: Berenice
people.summary: Daughter of Ptolemy II, married to Antiochus II to seal a peace between Egypt and Syria. When her father died her husband turned back to his first wife, Laodice, and Berenice and her son were murdered.
people.note: Not the Bernice of Acts 25. Daniel 11:6 foretold 'the daughter of the king of the south' who would not keep her power.
events: Marries Antiochus II, king of Syria
Is murdered with her son through Laodice's plotting

people.name: Ptolemy III
people.role: King of Egypt; 'king of the south'
people.summary: Brother of Berenice. He marched into Syria to avenge her murder, took the fortress of Antioch, put Laodice to death and carried rich spoil back to Egypt, including idols Persia had once taken.
people.note: Death year from general histories.
events: Becomes king and invades Syria to avenge his sister; takes Antioch's fortress
Brings home Egypt's old idols and treasure from Persia

people.name: Ptolemy IV
people.role: King of Egypt; 'king of the south'
people.summary: Defeated Antiochus III at Raphia and so kept Judah under Egypt, but did not press his victory and gave himself to a life of pleasure.
people.note: Death year from general histories.
events: Defeats Antiochus III at Raphia near Egypt's border; Judah stays under Egypt

people.name: Ptolemy V
people.role: King of Egypt; 'king of the south'
people.summary: Became king as a boy of five. In his reign Egypt lost Judah to Antiochus III, who then married his daughter Cleopatra I to him. He was poisoned while trying to win back the lands promised as her dowry.
people.note: Birth from his age when he became king; death year from general histories.
events: Becomes king at about five years of age
His army is beaten at Paneas, and Judah passes to Syria
Marries Cleopatra I, daughter of Antiochus III

people.name: Cleopatra I
people.summary: Daughter of Antiochus III, married to Ptolemy V so that her father could control Egypt through her. Instead she took her husband's side.
people.note: Death year from general histories.
events: Marries Ptolemy V; she sides with Egypt, not her father

people.name: Ptolemy VI
people.role: King of Egypt; 'king of the south'
people.summary: Son of Ptolemy V and Cleopatra I. When Antiochus IV invaded Egypt and made himself king there, he asked Rome for help, and Rome forced Antiochus out.
people.note: Death year from general histories.
events: Asks Rome for help against Antiochus IV

people.name: Seleucus I
people.role: King of Syria; the first 'king of the north'
people.summary: A general of Alexander who won Mesopotamia and Syria and founded the Seleucid dynasty, which ruled from Syria until Rome took it over in 64 B.C.E. He built Antioch, where Jesus' followers were later first called Christians.
events: Rules Mesopotamia and Syria, one of four parts of Alexander's empire
Founds Antioch, his new capital, and the port of Seleucia
Defeats Lysimachus but is assassinated the same year

people.name: Antiochus II
people.role: King of Syria; 'king of the north'
people.summary: Grandson of Seleucus I. To make peace with Egypt he set aside his wife Laodice and married Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II. Later he took Laodice back, and she poisoned him.
events: Divorces Laodice and marries Berenice of Egypt
Takes Laodice back, names her son his heir, and is poisoned by her

people.name: Laodice
people.summary: First wife of Antiochus II. Put aside for Berenice of Egypt, she won her place back, had Berenice and her son killed, and poisoned her husband, but was then killed by Berenice's brother Ptolemy III.
events: Has Berenice and her son murdered and poisons Antiochus II
Is put to death by Ptolemy III

people.name: Seleucus II
people.role: King of Syria; 'king of the north'
people.summary: Son of Antiochus II and Laodice. He struck back at Egypt but was defeated and limped home to Antioch with what was left of his army.
people.note: Death year from general histories.
events: Invades Egypt, is defeated, and retreats to Antioch

people.name: Seleucus III
people.summary: Son of Seleucus II. He gathered forces against Egypt but was murdered before he had reigned three years.
people.note: Death year from general histories.
events: Is assassinated; his brother Antiochus III takes the throne

people.name: Antiochus III
people.role: King of Syria; 'king of the north'
people.summary: The Seleucid king who took Judah from Egypt. Beaten at Raphia, he came back years later, won at Paneas, and took Jerusalem in 198 B.C.E. When he moved into Greece, Rome stepped in, defeated him and made him pay a heavy fine.
events: Succeeds his murdered brother as king
Takes Seleucia, Tyre, Ptolemais and many towns of Judah
Is defeated by Ptolemy IV at Raphia
Wins at Paneas, takes Sidon and then Jerusalem; Judah now belongs to Syria
Marries his daughter Cleopatra I to Ptolemy V
Beaten by the Romans at Magnesia and must give up Asia Minor
Dies while robbing a temple in Elymais, Persia

people.name: Seleucus IV
people.summary: Son of Antiochus III. Needing money to pay Rome, he sent his treasurer Heliodorus to seize the riches said to be kept in Jerusalem's temple. Heliodorus, wanting the throne, murdered him.
people.note: Death year from general histories.
events: Sends Heliodorus for the temple treasure in Jerusalem and is murdered by him

people.name: Antiochus IV
people.role: King of Syria who tried to wipe out Jewish worship
people.summary: Called himself Theos Epiphanes, 'God Manifest.' He sold the high priesthood, pushed Greek ways on the Jews, and in 168 B.C.E. defiled the temple and dedicated it to Zeus. Circumcision and the Sabbath were banned on pain of death. His persecution set off the Maccabean revolt.
people.note: Reign 175-164 B.C.E. (some sources say he died in 163). Some have tied him to Daniel 8 and 11, but Jesus spoke of 'the disgusting thing' of Daniel as still to come (Matthew 24:15).
events: Is put on the throne after his brother Seleucus IV is murdered
Sells the high priesthood to Jason and lets Jerusalem become a Greek city
Invades Egypt, but a Roman envoy draws a circle around him at Eleusis and orders him out
Defiles the temple: builds an altar to Zeus on the great altar, sacrifices a pig, and carries off the lampstand and altars
Bans circumcision and the Sabbath; Jews who refuse pagan sacrifice are killed

people.name: Onias III
people.summary: High priest in Jerusalem who lost his office when his brother Jason bribed Antiochus IV. In exile in Antioch he spoke out when Menelaus took money from the temple, and Menelaus had him murdered.
people.note: Year of death approximate.
events: Is replaced as high priest by his brother Jason
Condemns Menelaus' theft from the temple and is murdered

people.name: Jason (high priest)
people.role: High priest who brought in Greek ways
people.summary: Brother of Onias III. He bought the high priesthood from Antiochus IV, made Jerusalem a Greek city, and built a gymnasium where young Jews and even priests took part in the games. Three years later Menelaus outbid him.
people.note: Not the Jason of Acts 17 or Romans 16. Hebrew name: Joshua.
events: Bribes Antiochus IV for the high priesthood and builds a gymnasium in Jerusalem
Is outbid by Menelaus and flees
Hearing a rumor that Antiochus is dead, returns with 1,000 men to retake the office

people.name: Menelaus
people.summary: Perhaps not even of the priestly line, he bought the high priesthood with a bigger bribe than Jason's, paid for it with temple money, and arranged the murder of Onias III. He went on serving at the defiled temple.
people.note: Death year from general histories.
events: Outbids Jason for the high priesthood and takes money from the temple treasury
Arranges the murder of Onias III
Keeps serving at the temple Antiochus defiled

people.name: Mattathias
people.role: Priest of Modein; father of the Maccabees
people.summary: An aged priest of Modein, northwest of Jerusalem. Ordered to offer a pagan sacrifice, he refused, killed the Jew who stepped forward to do it and the king's officer, and fled to the hills with his five sons, calling everyone zealous for the Law to follow him.
people.note: Not the Mattathias in Jesus' genealogy (Luke 3:25, 26). His family are called Hasmonaeans, perhaps after an ancestor or the town of Heshmon (Joshua 15:27).
events: Refuses to sacrifice to the Greek gods at Modein and starts the revolt
Rules that Jews may fight to defend themselves on the Sabbath
Dies; his son Judas leads the revolt

people.name: Judas Maccabeus
people.summary: Son of Mattathias, nicknamed Maccabee, 'Hammer.' Using surprise attacks he beat much larger Syrian armies, retook Jerusalem, and rededicated the temple, which Jews still remember at Hanukkah. He then fought on for political independence and made a treaty with Rome, but was killed in battle.
events: Takes command of the revolt and wins battle after battle against larger armies
Retakes the temple, builds a new altar and rededicates it on Chislev 25; the festival of dedication begins

people.name: Jonathan Maccabeus
people.role: Leader of the Jews and high priest
people.summary: Took over after his brother Judas. By war and diplomacy he got the Syrian kings to make him high priest and ruler of Judea under them, though no Hasmonaean had held that office before. He was tricked, captured and killed by a Syrian plot.
people.note: Year he became high priest and year of death from general histories.
events: Leads the Jews after Judas' death
Is made high priest by the Seleucid rulers
Is lured into a trap by the Syrians and killed

people.name: Simon Maccabeus
people.role: Ruler and high priest of an independent Judea
people.summary: Last of the Maccabee brothers. Under him Judea threw off Seleucid rule, and in 140 B.C.E. the people named him leader and high priest for himself and his descendants. He was murdered at a banquet near Jericho by his son-in-law Ptolemy.
people.note: He called himself ethnarch, 'leader of the people,' not king.
events: Leads the Jews after Jonathan is killed
Frees Judea from Seleucid tribute; Jerusalem is the capital of a free land
A public decree makes him ruler and high priest 'until a trustworthy prophet should arise'
Murdered with two sons at a feast near Jericho

people.name: John Hyrcanus I
people.summary: Son of Simon. Once Syria was crushed by the Parthians, he enlarged Judea by conquest, made the Idumeans (Edomites) accept circumcision, and destroyed the Samaritans' temple on Mount Gerizim. The Pharisees and Sadducees first appear as parties in his day; he broke with the Pharisees and sided with the Sadducees.
people.note: Herod's family were Idumeans, so they were counted as Jews only because of his forced conversion.
events: Escapes the plot that killed his father and becomes ruler and high priest
Wins full independence after Syria loses a great battle to the Parthians
Conquers Idumea and forces the Edomites to be circumcised
Destroys the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim
Rebuked by the Pharisees, he breaks with them and backs the Sadducees

people.name: Aristobulus I
people.role: First Hasmonaean to call himself king
people.summary: Eldest son of John Hyrcanus. As high priest he also took the title of king, though he was not of David's line. In his single year of rule he brought upper Galilee under Jewish control and forced the Ituraeans to convert.
events: Forces the Ituraeans to accept Judaism and takes upper Galilee

people.name: Alexander Jannaeus
people.summary: Brother of Aristobulus I. Under him the Hasmonaean kingdom was at its largest. He openly called himself both king and high priest, fought a civil war against the Pharisees in which tens of thousands died, and had hundreds of rebels executed. He made Antipater, Herod's grandfather, governor of Idumea.
events: In a civil war with the Pharisees, about 50,000 Jews die and 800 rebels are executed
Dies, telling his wife Salome Alexandra to share power with the Pharisees

people.name: Salome Alexandra
people.summary: Widow of Alexander Jannaeus, chosen by him to rule instead of their sons. Her nine years were among the most peaceful of Hasmonaean rule. She gave the Pharisees back their influence. After her death her sons fought over the throne.
events: Becomes queen; brings the Pharisees back into power
Dies; her sons Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II fight for the throne

people.name: Hyrcanus II
people.summary: Elder son of Alexander Jannaeus and Salome Alexandra. A weak-willed man, he lost the throne to his brother and called on Rome for help. Rome left him as high priest while Antipater and his sons held the real power. Years later Herod, his grandson-in-law, had him killed.
people.note: Year of death from general histories; the sources say Herod killed him some years after taking Jerusalem.
events: Serves as high priest during his mother's reign
Fights his brother Aristobulus II for the throne, backed by Antipater
Asks Pompey to settle the dispute; Rome keeps him on as high priest
Has Herod tried before the Sanhedrin but gives in to pressure and drops the case
Is put to death by Herod

people.name: Aristobulus II
people.summary: Younger son of Alexander Jannaeus and Salome Alexandra. His fight with his brother Hyrcanus II for the throne brought the Roman general Pompey to Jerusalem and ended Jewish independence.
people.note: Death year from general histories.
events: Takes the throne from his brother
Pompey besieges Jerusalem for three months; about 12,000 Jews die

people.name: Alexander (son of Aristobulus II)
people.summary: Son of Aristobulus II. He married a granddaughter of Hyrcanus II's line, and their daughter Mariamne became Herod's wife.
people.note: Death year from general histories.

people.name: Antigonus
people.summary: Son of Aristobulus II and the last Hasmonaean to rule from Jerusalem. Herod took the city from him, and at Herod's urging Mark Antony had him killed.
events: Rules in Jerusalem as king and high priest
Loses Jerusalem to Herod and is put to death by Mark Antony

people.name: Antipater I
people.role: Governor of Idumea; grandfather of Herod
people.summary: The forefather of the Herods. The Hasmonaean king Alexander Jannaeus made him governor of Idumea.
events: Made governor of Idumea by Alexander Jannaeus

people.name: Antipater
people.role: Father of Herod the Great; governor of Judea
people.summary: A rich and scheming Idumean who backed Hyrcanus II while working for his own family's rise. Julius Caesar made him a Roman citizen and governor of Judea, and he set his sons Phasael and Herod over Jerusalem and Galilee. He was poisoned.
people.note: Death year from general histories.
events: Backs Hyrcanus II against Aristobulus II
Receives Roman citizenship and the governorship of Judea from Julius Caesar; makes Phasael governor of Jerusalem and Herod governor of Galilee

people.name: Cypros
people.summary: Wife of Antipater and mother of Herod, Phasael and Salome. With her daughter she kept up a bitter feud with Herod's wife Mariamne.

people.name: Phasael
people.role: Governor of Jerusalem; brother of Herod
people.summary: Elder brother of Herod, made governor of Jerusalem by their father Antipater.
people.note: Death year from general histories.
events: Made governor of Jerusalem by his father

people.name: Salome (sister of Herod)
people.summary: Herod's sister, who stirred up trouble in his family. When Herod lay dying and ordered leading Jews killed at his death, she and her husband Alexas set them free instead.
people.note: Not the Salome of the Gospels.
events: With her husband Alexas, frees the Jewish leaders Herod had shut in at Jericho

people.name: Mariamne I
people.summary: Granddaughter of Hyrcanus II and daughter of Alexander, son of Aristobulus II. Herod loved her deeply but, driven by suspicion, had her put to death, as he later did her two sons.
people.note: Years from general histories.
events: Is put to death on Herod's orders

people.name: Alexander (son of Herod)
people.summary: Son of Herod and the Hasmonaean Mariamne. Herod suspected him of plotting and had him executed, with his brother Aristobulus.
people.note: Year of death from general histories.

people.name: Aristobulus (son of Herod)
people.role: Son of Herod; father of Herodias and Herod Agrippa I
people.summary: Son of Herod and Mariamne, executed by his father with his brother Alexander. His children Herodias and Herod Agrippa I appear in the Bible.
people.note: Year of death from general histories. Not the Aristobulus of Romans 16:10.

people.name: Antipater (son of Herod)
people.summary: Herod's eldest son, a schemer against his half brothers. During his last illness Herod had him put to death.
events: Executed on Herod's orders during Herod's last illness

people.name: Pompey
people.summary: Roman general who ended the Seleucid kingdom by making Syria a Roman province. Called in to settle the quarrel between Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, he besieged Jerusalem for three months and took it, and from then on the Jews were under Rome.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Makes Syria a Roman province; the Seleucid dynasty ends
Takes Jerusalem after a three-month siege; Judea comes under Rome

people.name: Julius Caesar
people.summary: Roman general and statesman who made Herod's father Antipater governor of Judea. He was made dictator for ten years and murdered two years later. His adopted son Octavian became the emperor Augustus.
people.note: Birth year from general histories.
events: Gives Antipater Roman citizenship and the governorship of Judea
Is appointed dictator for ten years

people.name: Mark Antony
people.summary: Roman leader whose favor Herod won with large gifts. He had Antigonus executed at Herod's request, and Herod named his fortress by the temple, the Tower of Antonia, after him. He and Cleopatra VII lost to Octavian at Actium.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: At Herod's request has Antigonus put to death
Is defeated with Cleopatra at Actium by Octavian

people.name: Cleopatra VII
people.summary: The last of the Greek rulers of Egypt and the last 'king of the south' of that line. With her Roman lover Mark Antony she was defeated at Actium, and after her suicide Egypt became a Roman province.
people.note: Birth year from general histories.
events: Her forces and Antony's are defeated at Actium
Takes her own life; Egypt becomes a Roman province

people.name: Gaius (Caligula)
people.summary: Third Roman emperor, after Tiberius. Like the emperors before and after him he bore the name Caesar, which by now had become a title for the ruler of Rome.
people.note: Birth year from general histories.

people.name: Clement of Rome
people.summary: One of the Apostolic Fathers, writers who may have known an apostle. He quoted the Apocrypha as if it were inspired, seemed to know Christ more from writings outside the Gospels, and offered the myth of the phoenix as proof of the resurrection.
people.note: Year of birth not given in the sources; placed by generation. Year of death approximate.
events: About this time writes to the congregation in Corinth

people.name: Ignatius of Antioch
people.summary: One of the Apostolic Fathers. About a decade after the apostle John died, he wrote that each congregation should have one bishop presiding “in the place of God” over the elders. That idea opened the way for a clergy class.
people.note: Year of birth not given in the sources; placed by generation. Year of death approximate.
events: Writes that one bishop should preside over the elders of each congregation

people.name: Nero
people.role: Roman emperor; the 'Caesar' Paul appealed to
people.summary: The Caesar of the later chapters of Acts. Paul, on trial before Festus, appealed to him as a Roman citizen. After the great fire of Rome in 64 C.E. he blamed the Christians, and a wave of persecution by the state followed. The Jewish revolt broke out two years before he took his own life.
people.note: Birth from his age at death, about 31.
events: Paul, on trial before Festus, appeals to Caesar
Blames the Christians for the great fire of Rome; persecution follows
Takes his own life at about 31

people.name: Vespasian
people.summary: Became emperor in 69 C.E., the year after Nero's death. Under his rule his son Titus crushed the Jewish revolt and destroyed Jerusalem, and Rome struck coins reading 'Judea captured.'
people.note: Birth year from general histories.
events: Rome celebrates the conquest of Judea with coins reading 'Judea captured'

people.name: Flavius Josephus
people.summary: A Jewish historian from a priestly family and a Pharisee, who commanded rebels in Galilee during the revolt against Rome. After Jerusalem fell he wrote in Rome. Next to the Bible, his books are the main record of first-century Jerusalem and its temple, and they mention Jesus, James and John the Baptist.
people.note: Birth and death years approximate.
events: Is defeated in Galilee and surrenders to Vespasian, taking the family name Flavius
Sees Jerusalem destroyed, then goes with Titus to Rome to write his histories

people.name: Titus (Roman general)
people.role: Roman general who destroyed Jerusalem; later emperor
people.summary: Son of Vespasian. In 70 C.E. he besieged Jerusalem, crowded with Passover visitors, and fenced it in as Jesus had foretold. His offers of peace were refused, the temple was burned against his orders, and the city was razed. The Arch of Titus in Rome shows the temple vessels carried off. Not the Titus of Paul's letters.
people.note: Birth year from general histories.
events: Besieges Jerusalem and walls it in; the city and temple are destroyed

people.name: Akiba ben Joseph
people.summary: An esteemed rabbi, the first to give the many oral traditions a set form and structure, a work later finished in the Mishnah. In 132 C.E. he hailed Bar Kokhba as the Messiah. He and many of his disciples died when the revolt was crushed.
people.note: Birth and death years approximate.
events: Gives the oral traditions a set form and structure
Hails Simeon Bar Kokhba as the King Messiah
Dies with many of his disciples in the failed revolt

people.name: Domitian
people.summary: Son of Vespasian and brother of Titus, and a harsh opponent of Christianity. The apostle John is thought to have been exiled to Patmos in his reign, where he received the Revelation; tradition says John was freed after Domitian died.
people.note: Birth year from general histories.
events: Becomes emperor after his brother Titus
Dies; by tradition John is then freed from Patmos

people.name: Nerva
people.summary: Emperor after Domitian, ruling when the aged apostle John was alive and writing.
people.note: Birth year from general histories.

people.name: Cestius Gallus
people.role: Roman general who withdrew from Jerusalem
people.summary: Led the Twelfth Legion against Jerusalem in 66 C.E. His troops reached the temple walls, then he withdrew for no clear reason. That gave Christians the chance to obey Jesus' warning and flee before the Romans returned.
people.note: Death year from general histories.
events: Surrounds Jerusalem, reaches the temple walls, then suddenly withdraws

people.name: Eleazar (son of Jairus)
people.role: Leader of the dagger men at Masada
people.summary: Commander of the Sicarii, or 'dagger men,' a band of violent Jewish rebels. They took Masada from its Roman garrison in 66 C.E. and held it until 73, when, as the Romans broke through, he urged the defenders to die rather than surrender.
events: Seizes Masada and kills its Roman garrison
Masada falls; he and the defenders die rather than be captured

people.name: Shalmaneser III
people.role: King of Assyria in Jehu's day
people.summary: The first Assyrian king whose records mention Israel. His inscriptions confirm that Hazael seized the throne of Damascus, and his Black Obelisk names Jehu of Israel and shows tribute being brought to him, something the Bible does not record.
people.note: Years placed by Jehu's reign (c. 904-877 B.C.E.). His Karkar inscription names an 'Ahab the Israelite', but Insight doubts this is King Ahab, since it would not fit Bible chronology.
events: Records that Hazael killed his master and seized the throne of Damascus
Receives tribute from Jehu of Israel, pictured on his Black Obelisk

people.name: Adad-nirari III
people.summary: Assyrian king whose inscriptions tell of his attack on Damascus and of tribute from Jehoash of Samaria. He may have been the king of Nineveh who repented at Jonah's warning, but that is not certain.
people.note: Years assumed, placed by Jehoash of Israel and Jonah's mission (about 844 B.C.E.).
events: Attacks Damascus and receives tribute from Jehoash of Samaria
Possibly the king of Nineveh who repents at Jonah's preaching

people.name: Nabopolassar
people.role: King of Babylon; father of Nebuchadnezzar
people.summary: A Chaldean who rebelled against Assyria and founded a new dynasty in Babylon. Allied with Cyaxares the Mede, he destroyed Nineveh. His son Nebuchadnezzar took over the government in the year of the battle of Carchemish.
people.note: Death year from Nebuchadnezzar's taking the throne in 625 B.C.E.; birth assumed.
events: Founds a new Chaldean dynasty in Babylon (about this year)
Meets Cyaxares at the captured city of Asshur; they become allies
With the Medes captures and destroys Nineveh
His son Nebuchadnezzar beats Egypt at Carchemish and takes over the government

people.name: Cyaxares
people.summary: Under him the Medes became Assyria's most dangerous rival. He took Asshur, allied himself with Nabopolassar of Babylon, and together they destroyed Nineveh and divided Assyria's lands.
events: Captures Asshur and allies himself with Nabopolassar

people.name: Ashur-uballit II
people.summary: After Nineveh fell he tried to keep Assyria alive from Harran. Driven out, he came back with an Egyptian army to retake the city, but failed, and the empire came to an end.
events: Tries to rule what is left of Assyria from Harran
With an Egyptian army tries and fails to retake Harran

people.name: Nabonidus
people.role: Last king of Babylon; father of Belshazzar
people.summary: Babylon's last supreme ruler, given to literature, art and religion. In his third year he made his firstborn son Belshazzar king in Babylon and went off to live at Tema in Arabia. He lost to Cyrus and fled to Borsippa, so he was not at Belshazzar's feast on the night Babylon fell.
people.note: Reigned some 17 years (556-539 B.C.E.) by cuneiform texts; birth and death assumed.
events: Makes Belshazzar king in Babylon and campaigns to Tema in Arabia
Beaten by Cyrus, flees to Borsippa while Babylon falls

people.name: Trajan
people.summary: The emperor after Nerva. His governor Pliny asked him how to treat the Christians of Bithynia, and the letters between them are among the earliest records outside the Bible of what Christians did and how Rome dealt with them.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Is asked by Pliny how to deal with the Christians in Bithynia

people.name: Tacitus
people.summary: Often called the greatest historian of ancient Rome. He had little regard for Christians, yet he recorded that Nero made them scapegoats for the fire of Rome, and that Christ was executed under Pontius Pilate. He also names Quirinius and Felix, people the Bible speaks of.
people.note: Birth and death years approximate.
events: About this time writes his Annals, which tell of Christ's execution under Pilate and Nero's cruelty to Christians

people.name: Papias of Hierapolis
people.summary: An overseer in Hierapolis and an associate of Polycarp. He valued what Jesus and the apostles had said above the writings of his day, and collected the Lord's sayings in five books. Yet he believed that in the Thousand Year Reign each grape would give a thousand quarts of wine.
people.note: Years not given in the sources; placed by generation.
events: Collects the sayings of the Lord from those who knew the apostles

people.name: Pliny the Younger
people.summary: A Roman author and governor of Bithynia, in what is now Turkey. He wrote to Emperor Trajan about the Christians there: he tried to make them curse Christ and worship the emperor's image, and executed those who refused. His letter shows how firm the early Christians were.
people.note: Birth and death years approximate.
events: Writes to Trajan asking how to deal with the Christians in Bithynia

people.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
people.summary: One of the Apostolic Fathers, said to have been taught by the apostles and others who knew Jesus. He quoted the Bible and seems to have tried to live by it, and he chose to die rather than give up his faith. Afterward some treated his bones as more precious than jewels.
people.note: Birth and death years approximate.
events: Refuses to give up his faith and dies a martyr

people.name: Suetonius
people.summary: A Roman historian who wrote the Lives of the Caesars, on the first 11 emperors. His account of Claudius tells of turmoil among the Jews in Rome, likely over Jesus, which fits the Bible's report that Claudius ordered the Jews out of Rome.
people.note: Birth and death years approximate.
events: About this time writes the Lives of the Caesars

people.name: Aquila of Pontus
people.summary: A Jewish proselyte from Pontus who made a new and very literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures in the second century. Only fragments and quotations of it survive, among them in Origen's Hexapla.
people.note: Years not given in the sources; placed by generation.
events: Makes a very literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures

people.name: Marcion
people.role: Teacher who rejected the Hebrew Scriptures
people.summary: A rich young man who, less than 50 years after the apostle John died, publicly taught that Christians should reject the “Old Testament” and its God. Jesus and his apostles quoted those Scriptures as God's Word.
people.note: Years not given in the sources; placed by generation.
events: Publicly teaches that Christians should reject the “Old Testament”

people.name: Simeon Bar Kokhba
people.role: Commander of the Jewish revolt against Rome
people.summary: A mighty man with a powerful army who led the second Jewish revolt against Rome. Many Jews thought he was the Messiah who would free them. He failed, and hundreds of thousands of his people died with him.
people.note: Year of birth not given in the sources; placed by generation. Year of death approximate.
events: Leads the Jews in revolt against Rome

people.name: Justin Martyr
people.summary: A Greek philosopher born in Flavia Neapolis (now Nablus) who wrote in defense of Christianity. He mixed Scripture with Greek philosophy, taught that God has no proper name, and was followed by other Church Fathers, which sped the foretold apostasy. His writings show that he accepted the Jewish canon and rejected the Apocrypha.
people.note: Birth and death years approximate.
events: Converts to Christianity, possibly at Ephesus
Writes his Apologies, joining Scripture with Greek philosophy

people.name: Tatian
people.summary: A well-known writer of the second century from Syria who, in Rome, associated with Justin, perhaps as his pupil. He denounced the philosophers but called Christianity “our philosophy.” He was the first to give the congregations in Syria the Gospels in their own language, woven into one account, the Diatessaron. Later he joined the ascetic Encratites.
people.note: Years not given in the sources; placed by generation.
events: After Justin's death, joins or founds the Encratites
Weaves the four Gospels into one account, the Diatessaron

people.name: Irenaeus
people.summary: A professed Christian writer of the late second century. In Against Heresies he set out to refute the Gnostics, who claimed secret knowledge; it is the first work to mention a “Gospel of Judas.”
people.note: Born between 120 and 140 C.E.; year of death not given in the sources.
events: Writes Against Heresies, refuting the Gnostics

people.name: Judah ha-Nasi
people.role: Head of the Jewish community; compiler of the Mishnah
people.summary: A descendant of Hillel and Gamaliel, born during Bar Kokhba's revolt, and the last of the Tannaim. Fearing that wars with Rome would break the chain of oral teaching, he gathered the scholars of his day and had the oral law set down as the Mishnah.
people.note: Born during the revolt of 132-135; year of death not given in the sources.
events: Has the oral law put in writing: the Mishnah

people.name: Clement of Alexandria
people.summary: One of the best-known apologists. He saw philosophy as “true theology” and borrowed the idea of an immortal soul from Greek tradition. Origen was his pupil.
people.note: Birth and death years approximate.
events: Teaches in Alexandria that philosophy is true theology

people.name: Symmachus
people.summary: Translated the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek, probably about 200 C.E., aiming to give the sense rather than the words. His version filled one of the columns of Origen's Hexapla; no complete copy survives.
people.note: Years not given in the sources; placed by generation.
events: About this time translates the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek

people.name: Tertullian
people.summary: A prolific writer of the second and third centuries, drawn to Christianity by the courage of its martyrs. He asked what the Academy had to do with the church, yet he went beyond what is written: his formula “one substance in three persons” became a base for the Trinity doctrine.
people.note: Birth year approximate; year of death not given in the sources.
events: Coins the formula “one substance in three persons”

people.name: Origen
people.summary: A noted scholar of Alexandria and a pupil of Clement. His Hexapla kept God's name in Hebrew letters, but he mixed the Bible with Plato's ideas, teaching the “eternal generation” of the Son and the immortal soul, and opposed belief in a coming Thousand Year Reign.
people.note: Birth and death years approximate.
events: At 18 is made head of the school for religious instruction in Alexandria
Is stripped of his priesthood and moves to Palestine
Completes the Hexapla, which keeps God's name in Hebrew

people.name: Cyprian
people.summary: A bishop of Carthage, North Africa, who strongly backed the authority of the bishops as a class apart from the elders, the deacons and the laity. From his time, the clergy and the laity were separate.
people.note: Year of birth not given in the sources; placed by generation. Year of death approximate.
events: Sets the bishops apart as a class above elders, deacons and laity

people.name: Diocletian
people.summary: A Roman emperor who tried to destroy the Scriptures. In 303 C.E. he began a series of ever harsher edicts against Christians, the first ordering their Bibles burned and their meeting places torn down. Thousands of ancient Bible manuscripts survived anyway.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Orders copies of the Scriptures burned and Christian meeting places torn down

people.name: Arius
people.summary: A churchman of Alexandria who taught that the Son had a beginning and was not equal to God. The dispute over his teaching split the church, and Constantine called the Council of Nicaea to settle it. Arius was condemned there, but his followers remained strong for centuries.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: His teaching is condemned at the Council of Nicaea

people.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
people.summary: Known as the father of church history. His Ecclesiastical History tells that Christians fled Jerusalem to Pella before its destruction, as Jesus had warned. Excommunicated for holding that Christ is subordinate to the Father, he gave way at Nicaea, apparently caring more for his position than for Bible truth.
people.note: Birth and death years approximate.
events: At Nicaea supports the view he had opposed, as adviser to Constantine

people.name: Constantine the Great
people.summary: Roman emperor who ended the state's persecution of Christians and made the church a partner of the empire. Though still unbaptized, he presided at the Council of Nicaea and pushed it toward the idea that Jesus is equal with God. He was baptized only shortly before he died.
people.note: Birth year approximate.
events: Defeats his rival at the Milvian Bridge, claiming he saw a sign of the cross
With his co-ruler grants Christians freedom of worship
Calls and presides over the Council of Nicaea

people.name: Athanasius
people.summary: A churchman from Alexandria who supported Constantine's view at Nicaea and helped shape the ideas behind the Trinity. The creed named after him was written by someone else, probably in the fifth century, and was unknown in the East until the 12th century.
people.note: Birth year not given in the sources; placed by generation.
events: Backs Constantine's view at the Council of Nicaea

people.name: Theodosius I
people.summary: Roman emperor who made the Nicene creed the standard for his realm and called the Council of Constantinople, which put the holy spirit on the same level as God and Christ.
people.note: Years not given in the sources; placed by generation.

people.name: Damasus I
people.summary: The pope who saw Jerome's skill with languages and made him his secretary. With many careless Latin versions in use, he asked Jerome for an accurate revision of the Latin Gospels, the start of what became the Vulgate.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Makes Jerome his secretary and asks him to revise the Latin Gospels

people.name: Ulfilas
people.summary: A descendant of captives taken by the Goths, sent as a missionary to them. Gothic was not a written language, so he created a Gothic alphabet of 27 letters and translated the Bible. His version was used by the Goths who moved into Spain and Italy.
people.note: Birth and death years approximate.
events: Is ordained by Eusebius of Nicomedia to work among the Goths
Has translated the Bible into Gothic, using an alphabet he created

people.name: Jerome
people.summary: A scholar who became secretary to Pope Damasus and was asked to revise the Latin Gospels. He then settled in Bethlehem, learned Hebrew and translated the Hebrew Scriptures straight from it. His Latin Vulgate was the Western church's Bible for over a thousand years.
people.note: Year of death not given in the sources.
events: Completes his Latin translation of the Bible

people.name: Augustine of Hippo
people.summary: A Neoplatonist who converted at 33 and kept thinking like one, fusing the New Testament with Plato's philosophy. He taught that the Thousand Year Reign had already begun with the church, and that the church is now the kingdom of Christ, so watching for Christ's Kingdom seemed pointless.
events: Completes The City of God, teaching that the church is God's Kingdom

people.name: Leo I
people.summary: One of the first bishops of Rome to press his authority over the whole church. He took the old pagan title Pontifex Maximus and claimed spiritual power in the West while the emperor ruled from Constantinople.
people.note: Birth year not given in the sources; placed by generation.

people.name: Clovis I
people.summary: A pagan king of the Franks whose Catholic wife, Clotilda, urged him to convert. He chose Catholicism rather than Arianism, which bound his kingdom to the Church of Rome; the Encyclopædia Britannica calls it a decisive moment in the history of western Europe.
people.note: Birth year approximate.
events: Vows to give up paganism if his wife's God gives him victory, and is baptized a Catholic
Defeats the Visigoths at Vouillé and rules most of Gaul

people.name: Justinian I
people.summary: An emperor of the Byzantine Empire, which some historians date from his reign. His compilation of law, the Corpus Juris Civilis, became the base of Roman law in continental Europe. He fought the Arian kingdoms in the West but did not end Arianism.
events: Has Roman law compiled in the Corpus Juris Civilis
Sends his armies against the Arian rulers of Italy

people.name: Gregory I
people.summary: The pope who made the fire of purgatory a matter of unquestioned belief and has been called the inventor of purgatory. He also told missionaries to turn pagan temples into churches instead of destroying them, so that pagans would keep coming to their old places of worship.
people.note: Birth year from general histories.
events: Becomes pope and presses belief in purgatory
Tells a missionary to Britain to turn pagan temples into churches

people.name: Muhammad
people.summary: Born in Mecca, he said he received revelations from God through an angel, which were later written down as the Koran. After years of opposition in Mecca he moved to Medina, and in 630 Mecca surrendered to him. Within a century of his death Islam had reached Spain.
people.note: Birth year approximate.
events: Begins to receive what he says are revelations

people.name: Abu Bakr
people.summary: A close companion of Muhammad and his father-in-law, chosen to lead the Muslims when Muhammad died. Shiites hold that the leadership should have gone to Ali instead.
people.note: Years not given in the sources; placed by generation.
events: Is chosen as the first caliph

people.name: Ali
people.summary: Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law. Shiites believe he was Muhammad's rightful heir. He became the fourth caliph but was murdered.
people.note: Birth year not given in the sources; placed by generation.

people.name: Husayn
people.summary: Son of Ali and grandson of Muhammad. His death at the hands of Umayyad troops is mourned by Shiites to this day and sealed the split between Sunnis and Shiites.
people.note: Birth year not given in the sources; placed by generation.

people.name: Alcuin
people.role: Scholar who revised the Latin Bible
people.summary: A scholar of the eighth and ninth centuries who, with others such as Theodulf, set about correcting the errors that repeated copying had brought into Jerome's Latin Vulgate.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Presents a corrected text of the Latin Bible

people.name: Methodius
people.role: Bible translator; missionary to the Slavs
people.summary: A brother of Cyril, born to a noble family in Thessalonica. With Cyril he took the Scriptures to the Slavs of Moravia. After Cyril's death he went on with the work, despite opposition from Frankish clergy who wanted only Latin used.
events: Begins the mission in Moravia with his brother Cyril
Is arrested by the Frankish bishop Hermanrich
Dies; his disciples are expelled from Moravia

people.name: Cyril
people.role: Bible translator; missionary to the Slavs
people.summary: A scholar from Thessalonica who, with his brother Methodius, went to Moravia when its prince asked for teachers of the Scriptures. The Slavs had no written language, so he devised an alphabet and translated the Bible. Today over 360 million people use the Cyrillic alphabet descended from their work.
events: Begins the mission in Moravia with a new Slavonic alphabet
Goes to Rome to seek the pope's support

people.name: Gregory VII
people.summary: The pope who refused the duke of Bohemia's request to use Slavonic in church services. He wrote that God had made the Scriptures obscure in places so that common people would not misunderstand them.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Refuses to let Bohemia use Slavonic in church services

people.name: Urban II
people.role: Pope who called the First Crusade
people.summary: At a council in Clermont, France, he urged Europe's Christians to march east and win back the Holy Land from the Muslims, starting the Crusades.
people.note: Years not given in the sources; placed by generation.
events: Calls for the First Crusade at Clermont

people.name: Peter Waldo
people.summary: A merchant from Lyons, France, who in the 12th century paid scholars to translate the Bible into the language of southern France. His followers, the Waldenses, preached from it.
people.note: Years not given in the sources; placed by generation.
events: Has the Bible translated into the language of southern France

people.name: Gregory IX
people.summary: The pope who set up the papal Inquisition in 1231. It answered only to him, was staffed mostly by Dominican and Franciscan friars, and burned those it condemned as heretics.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Gives new force to the Inquisition at the Synod of Toulouse

people.name: Stephen Langton
people.summary: An English cleric who, while teaching in Paris early in the 13th century, divided the Bible into the chapters still used today. He later became Archbishop of Canterbury.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Divides the Bible into chapters while teaching in Paris

people.name: Innocent III
people.summary: A pope who applied Jesus' words about not throwing pearls before swine to ordinary people who read and discussed the Bible. He launched the Albigensian Crusade, the first crusade by Christendom against people who called themselves Christians.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Writes that the unlearned must not presume to study the Scriptures

people.name: Thomas Aquinas
people.summary: A 13th-century Catholic authority who so admired Aristotle that he called him “the Philosopher” and worked to merge Aristotle's ideas with church teaching. That blend later set the church against Galileo.
events: Works to merge Aristotle's philosophy with Catholic teaching

people.name: John Wycliffe
people.summary: An Oxford scholar who spoke out against the wealth and power of the church and wanted the Bible in the language of the people. He and his helpers produced the first English Bible, and his preachers, the Lollards, spread it. Decades after his death the church had his bones dug up and burned.
people.note: Born about 1328-1330.
events: Studies at Oxford and becomes master of Balliol College
Is summoned to answer for his teaching
The Christian Greek Scriptures in English are complete

people.name: Nicholas of Hereford
people.summary: A follower of John Wycliffe who did much of the work on the first complete English Bible, translated from the Latin Vulgate.
people.note: Years not given in the sources; placed by generation.
events: Helps Wycliffe produce the first complete English Bible

people.name: Jan Hus
people.summary: Rector of the University of Prague, strongly influenced by Wycliffe. He preached against the corruption of the church and the sale of indulgences and stressed reading the Bible. He was burned at the stake at the Council of Constance.
people.note: Birth year uncertain.
events: Is burned at the Council of Constance

people.name: Johannes Gutenberg
people.summary: A craftsman of Mainz, Germany, who worked out how to print with movable metal type. His first great work was the Latin Bible. Printing made the Bible and other books far cheaper, and it fed the Reformation.
people.note: Birth year approximate.
events: Prints the Latin Bible, about 180 copies

people.name: Mehmed II
people.summary: Ottoman sultan who besieged Constantinople and took it, ending the Byzantine Empire and making the city his capital.
people.note: Years not given in the sources; placed by generation.

people.name: Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros
people.role: Cardinal; adviser to Queen Isabella I of Spain
people.summary: The political and spiritual adviser of Isabella I of Spain, who founded the University of Alcalá. He bought up Hebrew manuscripts and had scholars produce the Complutensian Polyglot, the Bible in its original languages side by side, to revive the study of the Scriptures.
people.note: Birth year from general histories.
events: Decides to publish a Bible in the original languages, the Complutensian Polyglot
Sees the six volumes completed four months before his death

people.name: Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples
people.summary: A French scholar who turned from philosophy to the Bible because he wanted ordinary people to know God's Word. He published the Gospels in French in 1523 and the whole Greek Scriptures the next year; the Sorbonne objected, and his translation was later banned.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Publishes five Latin versions of the Psalms side by side
His French Bible is printed in Antwerp, the first in one volume

people.name: Frederick of Saxony
people.summary: The ruler of Saxony who protected Martin Luther. After the Diet of Worms he had Luther seized in a make-believe kidnapping and hidden in the Wartburg, where Luther translated the Greek Scriptures into German.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Has Luther “kidnapped” and hidden in the Wartburg

people.name: John Tetzel
people.summary: A Dominican friar who sold indulgences near Wittenberg in 1517, partly to pay for rebuilding St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. His sales moved Martin Luther to post his 95 theses.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Sells indulgences at Jüterbog, near Wittenberg

people.name: Desiderius Erasmus
people.role: Scholar and editor of the Greek New Testament
people.summary: The most admired scholar in Europe in his day, later called a coward by some and a heretic by others. He mocked the clergy's pomp and the popes' wars, and wanted Christianity to be a way of life. His Greek New Testament of 1516 was the first ever released in print, and translators such as Tyndale and Luther used it.
people.note: Birth year approximate.
events: Publishes the first printed Greek New Testament

people.name: Alfonso de Zamora
people.summary: The son of a rabbi who became a Catholic so as to stay in Spain after the Jews were expelled in 1492. One of the foremost Hebrew scholars of his day, he prepared the Hebrew text of the Complutensian Polyglot and translated the Hebrew Scriptures into Latin.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Becomes head of Hebrew studies at Alcalá and prepares the Polyglot's Hebrew text

people.name: Leo X
people.summary: The pope in Luther's day. He answered the 95 theses by threatening Luther with excommunication; Luther burned the papal bull in public, and in 1521 the pope excommunicated him.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Threatens Luther with excommunication unless he recants

people.name: Paul IV
people.summary: The pope who published the first index of forbidden books in 1559. It banned Bibles in English, French, German, Dutch, Italian and Spanish; anyone who wanted to read one needed a bishop's or inquisitor's permission.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Publishes the first Index of Forbidden Books

people.name: Thomas More
people.summary: Commissioned by the bishop of London to attack Tyndale in writing. He was upset that Tyndale rendered words as “congregation” and “elder” instead of “church” and “priest,” and he promoted the burning of “heretics.” He was himself beheaded after falling out with the king.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Is beheaded after falling out with Henry VIII

people.name: Martin Luther
people.role: German monk; leader of the Reformation
people.summary: An Augustinian monk who protested the sale of indulgences and taught that people are saved by faith. Excommunicated by the pope, he translated the Bible into German, and his work shaped the German language. His later essays against Jews who would not convert have led many to call him anti-Semitic.
events: Is excommunicated and stands trial at Worms
Completes the Hebrew Scriptures in German

people.name: William Tyndale
people.summary: An English scholar who wanted even a plowboy to know the Scriptures. Refused help in England, he translated and printed the Bible on the Continent and had it smuggled home. He was betrayed, then strangled and burned. Much of his wording lives on in later English Bibles.
people.note: Birth year approximate.
events: His New Testament reaches England; the bishops burn copies

people.name: Menno Simons
people.summary: A Catholic priest in the Netherlands who joined the Anabaptists in his search for truth. Hunted with a price on his head, he gathered believers into congregations, and his followers became known as Mennonites.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Breaks with the Catholic Church and joins the Anabaptists
Emperor Charles V offers a reward for his capture

people.name: Antonio Brucioli
people.summary: A humanist with Protestant leanings who never left the Catholic Church. In 1532 he published in Venice the first Italian Bible translated from the Hebrew and Greek; in some places and editions it restored God's name as “Ieova.”
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Publishes the first Italian Bible translated from the original languages

people.name: Charles V
people.role: Holy Roman Emperor and king of Spain
people.summary: A staunch Catholic who ruled the Holy Roman Empire and Spain. He tried Luther at the Diet of Worms, put a price on Menno Simons' head, and refused Francisco de Enzinas permission to circulate his Spanish New Testament.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Tries Luther at the Diet of Worms
Puts a price on Menno Simons' head
Refuses to allow Enzinas' Spanish New Testament

people.name: Robert Estienne
people.summary: A printer and scholar of Paris, printer to King Francis I. He produced careful editions of the Vulgate and the first critical edition of the Greek Scriptures, and in 1553 published the first complete Bible with basically the chapters and verses used today.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Takes over his father's press in Paris
Publishes the first complete Bible with today's chapters and verses

people.name: Olivétan
people.summary: Pierre Robert, called Olivétan, a young teacher from Picardy and a cousin of John Calvin. The Waldenses paid for a French Bible translated from the Hebrew and Greek, and he finished it in about a year. It was printed at Neuchâtel in 1535. He died in his early 30's.
people.note: Birth year approximate (he died in his early 30's).
events: Completes his French Bible from the Hebrew and Greek; it is printed at Neuchâtel

people.name: John Calvin
people.summary: A French reformer whose book Institutes laid the base for much of Protestant belief, including predestination. From Geneva he ran a strict religious state. Refugees there produced the Geneva Bible.

people.name: Huldrych Zwingli
people.summary: A Catholic priest in Zurich who taught himself Greek, read Erasmus and copied much of Paul's letters by hand. From about 1519 he attacked indulgences, the worship of Mary and clerical celibacy. He became a political force, and died as an army chaplain in a war between Catholic and Protestant Swiss.
events: Begins attacking indulgences and other church teachings in Zurich
Is killed in the battle of Kappel

people.name: Miles Coverdale
people.summary: A Catholic priest who began preaching against image worship and the Mass, and learned Bible translating from William Tyndale. His Bible of 1535 was the first complete printed English Bible, and his Great Bible was placed in England's churches. He fled when Catholic Mary became queen.
people.note: Birth year likely; year of death from general histories.
events: Publishes the first complete printed English Bible
His Great Bible is put in churches; it uses the name Jehovah

people.name: Thomas Cranmer
people.summary: The first Protestant Archbishop of Canterbury, who annulled Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon. Under Queen Mary he was condemned as a heretic; he recanted, but at the end publicly took it back and was burned.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Annuls Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine
Is burned as a heretic under Queen Mary

people.name: Jacob van Liesvelt
people.summary: The most prolific printer of Dutch Bibles, with 18 editions. His complete Dutch Bible of 1526 came years before the first complete printed Bibles in French and English. A note in his last edition, “Salvation comes through Jesus Christ alone,” was used to condemn him to death.
people.note: Year of birth not given in the sources; placed by generation.

people.name: Henry VIII
people.summary: King of England who first wrote against Luther and was named Defender of the Faith by the pope, then broke with Rome when the pope would not end his marriage, making himself head of the church in England.
people.note: Years not given in the sources; placed by generation.

people.name: Michael Servetus
people.role: Spanish scholar who rejected the Trinity
people.summary: A Spanish scholar who read the Bible in secret as a law student and concluded that Christianity had been corrupted in its first three centuries. At 20 he published On the Errors of the Trinity. John Calvin, his bitterest enemy, denounced him, and he was burned at the stake in Geneva.
events: Publishes On the Errors of the Trinity
Is burned at the stake in Geneva

people.name: Mary I
people.summary: The daughter of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon, raised a devout Catholic. As queen she brought England back to Catholicism; in less than four years at least 277 people were burned at the stake, and some 800 Protestants fled abroad.
events: Becomes queen and returns England to Catholicism
Protestants begin to be burned at the stake

people.name: Francisco de Enzinas
people.summary: A Spanish “Tyndale,” the son of a wealthy landowner, who translated the Greek Scriptures into Spanish while still a student and had them printed in the Netherlands. When he asked the emperor to allow them in Spain, he was soon imprisoned by the Inquisition.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Asks the emperor to allow his Spanish New Testament and is imprisoned

people.name: Casiodoro de Reina
people.summary: A monk near Seville who came to love the Bible and fled the Inquisition. Hunted even in London, he finished his translation of the whole Bible in about ten years; it was published in Basel in 1569 and used God's name, Jehovah. Thanks largely to him, readers of almost any Spanish Bible can see that God has a name.
people.note: Birth and death years approximate.
events: The Inquisition burns his effigy in Seville
Publishes his Spanish Bible in Basel

people.name: Christophe Plantin
people.summary: A bookbinder from France who became a pioneer printer in Antwerp. With the backing of King Philip II he printed the Royal Bible, a monumental Polyglot, between 1568 and 1572.
people.note: Birth year approximate; year of death from general histories.

people.name: Philip II
people.summary: The king of Spain who gave his full support to Plantin's revised Polyglot, the Royal Bible, and put Arias Montano in charge of it.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Backs the printing of the Royal Bible

people.name: Benito Arias Montano
people.role: Bible scholar; editor of the Royal Bible
people.summary: A Spanish Bible scholar who believed a translation should be as literal as possible. He edited the Antwerp Polyglot, or Royal Bible, using Alfonso de Zamora's manuscripts, and was denounced to the Inquisition for it.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Edits the Royal Bible in Antwerp

people.name: Szymon Budny
people.summary: A scholar of the Polish Brethren, asked to correct a poor Polish translation. He analyzed every word as no one in Poland had done, and published the whole Bible in 1572. In his Greek Scriptures he restored God's name in many places.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Begins work on a new Polish translation
Publishes his translation of the whole Bible

people.name: Cipriano de Valera
people.summary: Another former monk of Seville who escaped the Inquisition. He revised Reina's Bible, and his edition was printed in Amsterdam in 1602 and smuggled into Spain. The Reina-Valera Bible is still the most widely used among Spanish-speaking Protestants.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: His revision of Reina's Bible is printed in Amsterdam

people.name: Elizabeth I
people.summary: The daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn. She came to the throne in 1558 and reigned 44 years. Under her the Church of England became Protestant in practice, though it stayed largely Catholic in structure.
people.note: Year of death from general histories.
events: Becomes queen; the Church of England turns Protestant

people.name: Faustus Socinus
people.summary: An Italian, nephew of Laelius Socinus, who had been influenced by Servetus. He went to Poland and became prominent among the Polish Brethren, who rejected the Trinity and were also called Socinians.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Goes to Poland and becomes prominent among the Polish Brethren

people.name: Elias Hutter
people.summary: A German scholar of Oriental languages who became a professor of Hebrew before he was 24. His Hebrew Bible of 1587 used solid and outline letters to help students. His Nuremberg Polyglot gave the New Testament in 12 languages, with his own Hebrew translation that used God's name.
people.note: Year of death from general histories.
events: Publishes the Nuremberg Polyglot New Testament in 12 languages

people.name: Galileo Galilei
people.summary: An Italian astronomer who taught that the earth moves around the sun and held that this agrees with Scripture. He said he believed the Bible to be God's inspired Word, yet the Inquisition tried him in 1633 because the church followed Greek philosophy's view of the heavens. The Catholic Church admitted its error only in 1992.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Is tried by the Inquisition for teaching that the earth moves around the sun

people.name: James I
people.summary: King of Scotland who came to the English throne in 1603 and approved a new Bible translation, telling the translators to leave out offensive notes so that it would appeal to all. He was himself a respected Bible scholar. The King James Version, published in May 1611, bears his name.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Becomes king of England and approves a new Bible translation
The King James Version is published

people.name: William Bedell
people.summary: An English cleric who went to Ireland in 1627 and felt that the Irish should not have to learn English to know the Bible. He learned Irish himself and, from the early 1630s, translated the Hebrew Scriptures into Irish, using God's name in a number of places. His Bible was finished about 1640 but printed only in 1685.
people.note: Year of birth from general histories.
events: Goes to Ireland and insists on ministers who speak Irish
About this time begins translating the Hebrew Scriptures into Irish
About this time completes the translation
Is caught up in a rebellion against the English

people.name: Cyril Lucaris
people.summary: Born in Crete, he became patriarch of Alexandria and then of Constantinople. He wanted the Orthodox Church to return to the simplicity of the Bible, held that the Scriptures outrank the Church Fathers, and had the Greek Scriptures translated into the spoken Greek of his day. He gave the Codex Alexandrinus to the king of England. His enemies had him strangled in 1638.
events: Is banished to the island of Rhodes
Offers the Codex Alexandrinus as a gift to King James I
Publishes his Confession of Faith in Geneva; the monk Maximus begins a Modern Greek New Testament for him

people.name: Giovanni Diodati
people.summary: A Calvinist pastor whose parents had fled to Switzerland to escape religious persecution. In 1607 he published in Geneva another Italian Bible translated from the original languages.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Publishes his Italian Bible in Geneva

people.name: John Milton
people.summary: The English poet of Paradise Lost (1667), a retelling of man's fall. As a boy he studied the Bible in its original languages and came to see it as the only sure guide. Blind from 1652, he spent his last years on a treatise, On Christian Doctrine, that proved from the Bible that the soul can die and that the Son is subordinate to the Father. It was found only in 1823 and published two years later.
events: By now totally blind, keeps working on his treatise on Christian doctrine

people.name: Isaac Newton
people.summary: The famous English mathematician who spent perhaps more time studying the Bible than science. He showed that 1 John 5:7 and 1 Timothy 3:16, used to support the Trinity, had been altered, wrote that the earth would be inhabited for ever, and that Christ would return invisible to mortals. Fearing the law against denying the Trinity, he did not publish these findings.
events: Gives up his professorship at Cambridge to William Whiston
Dies; his work on the two altered texts is published only in 1754

people.name: Thomas Emlyn
people.summary: An English minister who served in Dublin. Careful Bible study convinced him that the Trinity is not taught there. When he confessed this in 1702 and published his proof that Jesus is not the Supreme God, he was tried for blasphemy, fined and imprisoned. He refused to retract, saying he suffered for God's truth.
events: Admits he no longer believes the Trinity
Is tried for blasphemy in Dublin and refuses to retract
Is released and moves to London

people.name: William Whiston
people.summary: A Cambridge colleague of Isaac Newton who succeeded him as professor of mathematics in 1702. Unlike Newton, he spoke out openly against the Trinity and was expelled from Cambridge in 1710. His translation of Josephus is still widely read, and he also translated the Christian Greek Scriptures.
people.note: Year of death from general histories.
events: Is ordained and becomes Newton's assistant at Cambridge
Succeeds Newton as professor of mathematics
Urges the archbishops to reform the teaching on the Trinity

people.name: John Wesley
people.summary: An English clergyman whose movement within the Church of England, begun in 1738, became the Methodist churches after his death.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Starts the movement that becomes Methodism

people.name: Joseph Priestley
people.summary: An English scientist who discovered oxygen in 1774. He held that tradition and dogma hinder religious truth, and he exposed widely held teachings as unscriptural. His views angered his countrymen, and he later fled to the United States.
people.note: Year of death from general histories.
events: A mob destroys his home and laboratory

people.name: William Carey
people.summary: A British shoemaker and teacher who in 1792 urged Christians to preach to other nations. In India, with Joshua Marshman and the printer William Ward, he produced at least parts of the Bible in nearly 40 languages.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Publishes his call for Christians to preach to other nations
About this time begins translating the Bible in India

people.name: Neofitos Vamvas
people.summary: A Greek linguist and Bible scholar who blamed the Orthodox Church for the people's ignorance of the Bible. He began translating it into Greek in 1831 and published the complete Bible in 1850; the church banned it.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Begins translating the Bible into Greek

people.name: Henry Grew
people.role: Bible student who rejected the Trinity
people.summary: Born in Birmingham, England, he moved to the United States as a boy. Rejected as a Baptist pastor because he held that only faithful men should lead in worship, he studied the Bible with a small group. He wrote against the Trinity, war, the immortal soul and hellfire, and his pamphlet set George Storrs studying.
events: Becomes pastor of the Baptist church in Hartford, Connecticut
Writes a refutation of the Trinity
About this time writes a pamphlet showing that the immortal soul and hellfire are not in the Bible

people.name: Robert Morrison
people.summary: A British missionary who sailed for China in 1807, determined to publish the whole Bible in Chinese. Teaching Chinese to foreigners was banned on pain of death, and printing Christian books became a capital crime, yet he finished the Christian Greek Scriptures in 1814 and the whole Bible on November 25, 1819.
people.note: Year of birth worked out from his age in 1807; year of death from general histories.
events: Sails for China to translate the Bible
Has the Christian Greek Scriptures ready for printing
Completes the whole Bible in Chinese

people.name: William Miller
people.summary: An American preacher who taught that Christ would return visibly in 1843. George Storrs preached his message for about two years.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Preaches that Christ will return visibly in 1843

people.name: Gerasim Pavsky
people.summary: A Russian Orthodox professor of Hebrew who translated the Hebrew Scriptures into Russian. He used the name Jehovah more than 35 times in the Psalms alone. After a complaint to the synod in 1841, copies of his translation were destroyed.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Finishes a Russian translation of the Psalms
An anonymous complaint is made to the synod about his translation

people.name: Adoniram Judson
people.summary: An American missionary who settled in Burma with his wife, Ann, in 1813. Though jailed in irons as a suspected spy, he finished the Burmese Christian Greek Scriptures in 1823 and the whole Bible in 1835.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.
events: Completes the Christian Greek Scriptures in Burmese
Completes the whole Bible in Burmese

people.name: Makarios
people.summary: A Russian Orthodox missionary, Mikhail Glukharev, who translated most of the Hebrew Scriptures into Russian and used the name Jehovah more than 3,500 times. The synod punished him for it. His Bible was printed only between 1860 and 1867, and Jehovah's Witnesses republished it in 1993.
people.note: Year of birth from general histories.
events: Arrives in St. Petersburg seeking permission to translate the Hebrew Scriptures
Is ordered to do penance for his translation work
Dies before he can publish his Bible abroad

people.name: George Storrs
people.summary: A Methodist minister who, after reading Henry Grew's pamphlet in 1837, left his church and taught that the soul is mortal. He published the Bible Examiner in Brooklyn, came to see that the unrighteous will be resurrected, and helped the young Charles Taze Russell, who called him a beloved brother.
events: Reads Henry Grew's pamphlet on a train
Gives six sermons asking whether the wicked are immortal
Concludes that the unrighteous will be resurrected with a chance of everlasting life

people.name: Robert Moffat
people.summary: A Scottish missionary who in 1821 set up a mission among the Tswana of southern Africa. He learned their unwritten language by living among them, finished the Gospel of Luke in 1829 and travelled some 600 miles to have it printed in Cape Town.
people.note: Year of birth worked out from his age in 1821; year of death from general histories.
events: Sets up a mission among the Tswana
Finishes translating Luke and has it printed in Cape Town

people.name: Frederick Parker
people.summary: A wealthy London businessman who rejected the Trinity and studied Greek. After seeing Shadwell's Matthew he revised his New Testament to use Jehovah. His 1863 edition, published under the name Herman Heinfetter, was the first English New Testament to restore God's name extensively.
events: Begins publishing his New Testament translation
Publishes a New Testament that uses the name Jehovah
Publishes an English version that uses God's name 186 times

people.name: Lancelot Shadwell
people.summary: An English barrister who believed God's name should be restored to the New Testament. Though he accepted the Trinity, he used Jehovah in his translation of Matthew in 1859, which moved Frederick Parker to do the same.
events: Publishes his translation of Matthew using the name Jehovah
Publishes Matthew and Mark, and dies

people.name: Konstantin von Tischendorf
people.summary: A German scholar convinced that early manuscripts would prove the Bible text genuine. He deciphered the Codex Ephraemi and, at St. Catherine's Monastery at Mount Sinai, found the Codex Sinaiticus, one of the oldest Bible manuscripts, and saved it from destruction.
events: Publishes what he deciphered of the Codex Ephraemi
Finds 129 leaves of an ancient Greek manuscript at St. Catherine's Monastery
On his third visit, obtains the Codex Sinaiticus

people.name: Jonas Wendell
people.summary: A Second Adventist preacher. Hearing him in a dusty hall in 1869 restored the young Charles Taze Russell's wavering faith that the Bible is God's Word.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.

people.name: George W. Stetson
people.summary: An earnest Bible student and pastor of the Advent Christian Church in Edinboro, Pennsylvania, who helped the young Charles Taze Russell study the Scriptures. Russell called him a man of marked ability and preached at his funeral.
people.note: Year of birth worked out from his age at death.
events: Dies; Russell preaches his funeral sermon

people.name: Benjamin Wilson
people.summary: Translator of The Emphatic Diaglott (1864), which used God's name in the Christian Greek Scriptures and rendered parousia as "presence," not "coming."
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.

people.name: Joseph Seiss
people.summary: A Lutheran minister in Philadelphia who wrote in 1856 that Christ's return would come in two stages: an invisible presence followed by a visible manifestation.
people.note: Birth and death years from general histories.

people.name: Nelson H. Barbour
people.summary: Editor of the Herald of the Morning in Rochester, New York. He believed that Christ's return would bless mankind and be invisible, and convinced Russell that Christ's presence began in 1874.
